name: Limburgish (Rheinische Dokumenta notation)

ancestors.notes: Same language as `li`; this spec only changes which written convention is modeled. The two conventions share almost no signs, so the grapheme table is stated in full rather than pulled in through `graphemes_base`: Rheinische Dokumenta is a separate sign inventory, not a re-accented Spelling 2003.

orthography_standard.name: Rheinische Dokumenta
orthography_standard.authority: LVR-Institut fuer Landeskunde und Regionalgeschichte (Landschaftsverband Rheinland), Koeln
orthography_standard.notes: A regional-authority transcription standard for the dialects of the Rhineland, published by the Landschaftsverband Rheinland's regional-studies institute and used in dialect dictionaries and dialect writing. It is a documentation notation rather than an everyday spelling norm, and it is not specific to Limburgish: it covers the Lower Rhine, the Rhineland, the Bergisches Land, the Westerwald, the Eifel and the Hunsrueck as one system. Limburgish falls inside that area, and part of the li/wikipron gold is written in it.

notes: Rheinische Dokumenta is the Landschaftsverband Rheinland's transcription standard for the dialects of the Rhineland, and part of the Limburgish gold this library is benchmarked against is written in it rather than in the Veldeke Spelling 2003 that `li` models. The two are disjoint sign systems, which is why this is a separate entry and not an accent variant: Spelling 2003 writes the postalveolar fricative as <sj> and has no <e-vertical-line>, <o-ogonek>, <s-dot> or <c-tie-h>, while Rheinische Dokumenta writes it as <sch> and has no <ae>, <ao>, <ee-grave> or <o-acute-w>. SIGN INVENTORY: nine signs carry a diacritic that separates them from a plain counterpart -- a-with-dot [ɑ] against a [a], a-ogonek-diaeresis [æ] against ä [ɛ], o-ogonek [ɔ] against o [o], oe-ogonek [œ] against ö [ø], e-with-vertical-line [ə] against e [e], s-with-dot [z] against s [s], r-with-dot [ʁ] against r, c-tie-h [ɣ] and c-caron-h [χ] against ch [x], and s-caron-ch [ʒ] against sch [ʃ]. LENGTH: the standard is phonemic and writes length by doubling the vowel sign, so every vowel sign has a doubled long counterpart. For i/o/ü the source table (English Wikipedia's Rheinische Dokumenta article) lists the cardinal quality first and the laxer realisation second; for u/uu it lists the LAX vowel first instead -- <u> [ʊ, u], <uu> [ʊː, uː], with sample words "put" [ʊ] and "boot" [uː] -- and that is the order followed here, uniformly across all four vowels, even though it costs PER against this gold (see MEASURED): the gold's own u/uu readings skew tense, but the source's ordering is followed rather than fitted to the gold. The ordering also matches the canonical Germanic short=lax/long=tense pairing (ɪ/iː, ʊ/uː, ʏ/yː). TONE IS NOT REPRESENTED: like Spelling 2003, Rheinische Dokumenta does not write the Limburgish sleeptoon/stoottoon contrast, so none is emitted. INPUT CONTRACT: text written in Rheinische Dokumenta with its diacritics intact. The diacritics carry the system; text that has lost them is indistinguishable from German-based ad-hoc spelling and will mis-transcribe. MEASURED: on the 89 li/wikipron gold headwords that carry a Rheinische-Dokumenta-exclusive sign, this entry scores PER 0.0609 against 0.3245 for `li`, and 58 of the 89 come out exactly right. Most of the residual traces to the u/uu ordering above: the gold's rheindok-tagged words consistently render <u>/<uu> as tense [u]/[uː] rather than the source's lax-first [ʊ]/[ʊː], which is a gold-vs-source disagreement rather than a defect in this table. A smaller share is symbol choice unrelated to vowel length: several words write the labial approximant with the labiodental symbol where the standard's sign list gives [w]/[β], and one writes a plain palatal glide where the sign list gives the fricative. Neither substitution is made here. No fetched primary description of Limburgish was available to justify either one, and guessing the gold's preference would be fitting rather than describing.
